list.listitem: Almost all infants exposed to prolonged in utero opioids will demonstrate some symptoms of withdrawal, with ~50% having signs and symptoms severe enough to require pharmacologic treatment. C

The use of a standardized symptom assessment instrument, such as the Finnegan score or Eat-Sleep-Console scale, is a key element in the diagnosis and management of neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS). C
Opioid replacement with methadone or buprenorphine is the preferred pharmacologic treatment. Morphine is also an option, but the former have been shown to be somewhat more effective.B
Adjunctive therapies include phenobarbital and clonidine. The optimal drug, dose, and regimen have not been defined. C
Institutions should have standardized pathways for diagnosis and management. C

background.definition: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) is a generalized disorder characterized by signs and symptoms of central nervous system (CNS) hyperirritability, GI dysfunction, respiratory distress, and autonomic dysfunction. In utero exposure to opioids can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS), with prolonged symptoms in infants requiring pharmacologic therapy. Some, but not all, other drugs of abuse may also cause limited withdrawal symptoms.

list.listitem: Opioid use disorder is present in 4 of 1000 pregnant women in 2011.
The use of illicit drugs in pregnant women decreases with age, with 15% use in 15- to 17-year-old women and dropping to 2% use in those older than 26 years.
The rate of NAS per 1,000 US births rose from 1.2 in 2000 to 6 in 2013, with some states >30.
The number of NAS hospital admissions increased 4-fold between 2003 and 2012. In 2012, the estimated cost burden of NAS in the US was $316 million.

In addition to NAS, neonatal complications of children born to women who are opioid dependant include postnatal growth deficiency, microcephaly, neurobehavioral problems, increased neonatal mortality, and a 74-fold increase in sudden infant death syndrome.
Maternal use of opioids during pregnancy can cause symptoms of withdrawal in the newborn. Pharmacologic therapy in neonates is used to ensure proper growth and development.
Cessation of placental transfer of maternal administered opioids leads to precipitous drops in neonatal blood concentrations.

In utero exposure to benzodiazepines, cocaine, nicotine, methamphetamines, antidepressants, and antipsychotics can cause transient irritability in the first few days of life, but generally do not require pharmacologic therapy.
Exact pathophysiology is not clear.
Opiates inhibit cAMP production in the CNS, with long term compensatory changes of increased adenylyl cyclase.
Rapid removal of opiates unmasks increased adenylyl cyclase activity, causing a marked rise in norepinephrine and a withdrawal symptom complex.

Illicit drug use should be considered possible in all pregnancies, with higher likelihood in mothers without prenatal care, history of sexually transmitted infection, or behaviors or stigmata (i.e., needle "tracks") of chronic drug use. C

Maternal self-report and urine drug screens will identify many, but not all, mothers who use narcotics or other illicit drugs. Legal issues surrounding maternal urine drug testing will vary with locale. C
Do not discontinue maternal methadone or buprenorphine to prevent NAS. Continuation of maintenance therapy during pregnancy leads to decreased illicit drug use and better neonatal outcomes. C
Suspect NAS in children presenting with signs of increased muscle tone, irritability, poor feeding, and loose stool, particularly if there is known or suspected maternal opioid use. C

NAS is diagnosed clinically. Infant urine drug screens are most accurate when collected as soon as possible following birth. Meconium and hair analysis may add sensitivity but are impractical in many clinical settings. C
All children with risk factors should have monitoring for symptoms of abstinence using a standard instrument. C

A standardized scoring instrument should be used in each nursery to identify infants with NAS of severity enough to require treatment, as well as to guide dose titration in those infants treated with pharmacologic agents (see ).
Specific scoring systems include those of Finnegan, Lipsitz, Ostrea, Green and Suffet and Zahorodny. The Finnegan score (or modifications of it) has been the most commonly used historically.

A short "Eat-Sleep-Console" scale based on three elements (eating, sleep quality, and consolability) has been recently developed, and studies suggest reduced time to readiness for hospital discharge compared to the Finnegan score (adjusted mean difference 6.7 days; 95% CI 4.7 - 8.8) without a difference in adverse events. As a result, many hospitals are transitioning to use of the Eat-Sleep-Console scale.

Infants born to mothers who use opioids during pregnancy are at risk. Most infants with prolonged in utero exposure will show signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal. Approximately 50% to 70% will have symptoms that require pharmacologic treatment.
Age at onset of symptoms is 4 to 24 hours for heroin and 24 to 72 hours for methadone and buprenorphine. Presentation as late as 10 days of age is possible.

Signs of NAS include irritability, difficulty sleeping, increased muscle tone, myoclonic jerks, yawning, poor feeding, failure to thrive, diarrhea, and skin excoriation. See for an example of an NAS scoring system.
The need for pharmacologic treatment is a clinical diagnosis using a standardized scoring instrument in at-risk infants. A representative scoring system is presented in .
NAS is diagnosed clinically. Assay of maternal urine for drugs of abuse is more useful than infant urine. Meconium and hair analysis may add sensitivity but have more limited availability.
Order cultures, CBC, serum glucose, serum calcium, and other tests as clinically indicated to rule out alternate diagnoses such as infection, hypoglycemia, and hypocalcemia.
All infants should receive non-pharmacologic therapy. See
Only those with severe disease should receive pharmacologic therapy. An opioid approach is presented in .
High quality evidence to support recommendations is limited. Opioid replacement is widely accepted as the preferred pharmacologic treatment of opioid-induced NAS.B
Randomized controlled trials suggest an efficacy advantage of buprenorphine or methadone over morphine and other agents for the treatment of neonatal abstinence syndrome.B

A short scale based on three elements (eating, sleep quality, and consolability) has been developed. A cluster randomized trial at 26 hospitals with 837 infants found that using this "Eat, Sleep, Console" approach reduced time to readiness for hospital discharge compared to the Finnegan score (adjusted mean difference 6.7 days; 95% CI 4.7 - 8.8) without a difference in adverse events.

Opiate replacement is the preferred pharmacologic treatment. Compared to supportive care, use of opioids reduces the time needed to regain birthweight and the need for supportive care, but appears to lengthen hospital stay. Opioids used in NAS are morphine, methadone, or buprenorphine (see ). The Cochrane review found no difference in outcomes for methadone vs morphine, and increased hospitalization days for morphine as compared with sublingual buprenorphine.

Two RCTs have found better results with methadone or buprenorphine compared to morphine. In a blinded RCT with 63 infants, sublingual buprenorphine was associated with a 42% decrease in length of treatment compared to oral morphine (15 vs. 28 days). In a multicenter RCT with 116 treated infants, methadone was associated with a modest reduction in median length of treatment compared with morphine (11.5 vs. 15 days).
A network meta-analysis of 18 clinical trials comparing opioids, clonidine, and phenobarbital concluded that buprenorphine was the preferred therapy and that morphine was the least effective.
There are varied methadone doses used, but a pharmacokinetic driven regimen has been associated with favorable outcomes.

In one RCT (N = 80), adding clonidine (1 mcg/kg every 4 hours) vs. placebo to morphine for infants with NAS reduced the length of therapy (11 vs. 15 days) and percentage of infants requiring higher opium doses (20% vs. 40%) despite 7 infants requiring restarting opium after initial discontinuation versus none in the placebo group. However, a Cochrane review concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the routine use of clonidine alone compared with opioids.

Phenobarbital is used as an adjunct to opioids at some institutions, or as a rescue medication. Sedation and induction of hepatic enzymes are adverse events associated with use. Use as monotherapy is inferior to opioid. A Cochrane review identified 10 studies but found that, while it may reduce days to regain birthweight and duration of supportive care, the body of evidence regarding its effectiveness is limited and any conclusions are low certainty.
Phenobarbital may be more efficacious than clonidine as an adjunct to opioid treatment, but the comparative short and long term safety between the two have not been defined.
Outside of acute treatment of NAS associated seizures, benzodiazepines should be avoided in the treatment of NAS.
Regardless of primary opioid used, adherence at the institutional level to a strict treatment protocol is a key predictor of improved outcomes.
Rooming in with mother in a quiet room is recommended.
Frequent, calorically dense feedings (24 kcal/oz) are also often recommended.
Swaddling is commonly used and is safe if properly applied.
However, a Cochrane review of 6 RCTs concluded that the evidence was insufficient to evaluate the effectiveness of these non-pharmacologic therapies.
Child protective services must evaluate the discharge social environment.
Breastfeeding by mothers maintained on methadone or buprenorphine is safe and should be encouraged, so long as there is no evidence of use of other illicit drugs.
Rooming-in may reduce the need for pharmacotherapy, but this is based largely on before/after and retrospective observational studies.
Duration of pharmacologic therapy should be guided by a validated scoring system ().
Mean length of stay using opioid replacement for NAS is 2 to 3 weeks.

In one study of 60 infants with NAS (median gestational age 39 weeks, range 26-42 weeks) following a change in hospital care policy, infants cared for on the postnatal ward with their mothers (N = 18, year 2006-2007) compared with infants assessed and cared for as necessary in the neonatal unit (N = 42, years 2002-2005) were less likely to require treatment for NAS (11% vs. 45%), had a shorter duration of treatment (mean 7.3 vs. 12.7 days), and had a shorter hospital stay (mean 15.9 vs. 19.8 days). No infant in either group was readmitted within the next 2 months.
Children should be observed for stability at least 48 hours following cessation of pharmacologic therapy.
Treatment with opioids should take place in the hospital for the majority of infants.

Outpatient treatment using opioids and/or phenobarbital is associated with shorter length of stay, but longer duration of total treatment and higher frequency of ED visits and hospitalization at 6 months.

Infants exposed to in utero opioids show low birthweight, increased preterm birth, reduced fetal growth parameters, and impaired neurodevelopmental delay, but studies generally do not control for tobacco and other social factors associated with illicit drug use. B
Opioids, as compared to supportive care only, appear to reduce the time to regain birth weight and reduce the duration of supportive care. They do not reduce the length of hospital stay. C
Treatment of NAS with opioids does not appear to have adverse developmental outcomes, but data are limited. B
Continued attention to abstinence scoring and weight are key elements, even following the cessation of pharmacologic therapy. C

algorithm.title: Identification and Treatment of Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome.

cell.label: Identify newborns who may have been exposed in utero to opioids or other drugs of abuse: maternal history, urine drug screen, infant drug screen, or suspicion of undisclosed drug use (lack of prenatal care, maternal stigmata of drug use, sexually transmitted disease).
Minimize stimuli, employ small calorically dense feedings, swaddle gently. Monitor for signs of neonatal abstinence using a standardized symptom instrument (). Scores require pharmacologic treatment?
Initiate morphine-containing regimen at 0.4 mg/kg/day in 6 divided doses. Titrate up 20%/day until symptoms controlled. Seizures?
Symptoms controlled and good weight gain before reaching maximum dose (~1.25 mg/kg/day morphine).
Wean 10%/day as guided by symptom scores. Infant with controlled symptoms?
When morphine is discontinued, monitor for at least 2 days in an inpatient setting prior to discharge from hospital.
Resume last dose at which symptoms controlled; wean as tolerated.
Phenobarbital load with daily dosing. Investigate possible non-withdrawal etiologies.
Monitor for 2-4 days as an inpatient prior to discharge.

feature.caption: Neonatal Abstinence Scoring Tool.
feature.feature_body: Assess infants every 3-4 hours before feeds. Reassess within the first hour after feeds. Consider initiation of pharmacologic treatment if the average of 3 consecutive scores is >12. Increase dose if the average of 3 consecutive scores is >12. Decrease dose if scores remain consistently <8. Unscored elements serve to provide additional detail regarding symptom severity. Data from Finnegan LP, Kaltenbach K. Neonatal abstinence syndrome. Hoekelman RA, Friedman SB, Nelson N, Seidel HM, eds. Primary Pediatric Care. Second ed. Mosby: St. Louis; 1992: 1367-1378.

feature.caption: Medications for Treatment of Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome.

tr.td: Morphine (oral solution)
Morphine equivalent of 0.4 mg/kg/day in 6 divided doses, 20%/day increase in dose for poorly controlled symptoms
Taper 10%/day
This has replaced tincture of opium and paregoric as morphine-containing solution
Methadone
0.05-0.1 mg/kg every 6 hours with increases of 0.05 mg/kg until symptoms controlled, after which drug is administered every 12-24 hours
Taper 0.05 mg/kg/day

Preparation contains 8% ethanol and there is a lack of standardized dosing and pharmacokinetic characterization of drug in infants. There are a number of different dose regimens reported in literature.
Phenobarbital
20 mg/kg loading dose; followed by 5 mg/kg day
Maintain dose until opioid weaned ~50% and then wean
Useful as adjunct in severe disease, in polydrug abuse, and treatment of seizure; potential for sedation. Therapeutic drug monitoring not helpful unless seizures present
Clonidine
1 mcg/kg po every 4 hours (administered with opioid)
Maintain until cessation of opioid
Generally well tolerated, but potential for hypotension and bradycardia during use and rebound sympathetic signs following cessation
Buprenorphine
15 mcg/kg/day in 3 divided doses, 25% increase for poorly controlled symptoms; maximum dose 60 mcg/kg/day
Taper 10% per day
Preparation contains 30% ethanol

feature.caption: Non-Pharmacologic Treatments for the Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome.

tr.th: Approaches may include many of the following

tr.td: •rooming in•swaddling •1:2 or 1:3 nurse to patient ratio. •quiet, low lighting, lower ambient temperature•lactation support•feeding on demand, if formula: low lactose •guidelines for skin care •parent education and support •volunteer cuddlers •physical/occupational therapy, targeted visual and auditory stimulation (music)
